chunks: "The classic PoP chips are mobile application processors: the SoC in a smartphone or tablet, with LPDDR DRAM stacked on top.

Many phone SoCs from the big mobile vendors have been sold or built that way, and some compact single-board computers and small embedded boards have used the same trick, for example the original Raspberry Pi stacked its SDRAM on top of the Broadcom processor.
You also see it in other area-constrained, battery-powered products like wearables, cameras and some automotive infotainment modules. Why those?
Because they have the right mix of constraints. Board area and thickness are tight, so stacking the memory saves the footprint of a separate package.
They use LPDDR, a wide, fast interface where a very short connection saves power and eases timing: a couple of millimetres through two substrates instead of 25 millimetres of PCB route.
Their power is low enough, a few watts, that the thermal penalty from putting memory on the hot die is manageable.
And the volumes are huge, so a standardised stack that a vendor tests as a unit is cheap and easy to ship.
On the other side, you don't see PoP on servers, desktop CPUs, GPUs or big FPGAs.

They dissipate tens to hundreds of watts and need big heat sinks on the die; they need more memory capacity and flexibility than a stacked package gives, and their bandwidth needs go to DIMMs, GDDR or HBM instead.
So the short answer is: low-power, area-constrained, high-volume SoCs with LPDDR."
